A_target.statement:
Let $G$ be a [[Definition:Finite Group|finite group]] and $p$ a [[Definition:Prime Number|prime]] with $p^a \divides \order G$.
Then $G$ has a [[Definition:Subgroup|subgroup]] of order $p^a$.

B_source.statement:
Let $G$ be a [[Definition:Finite Group|finite group]] and $p$ a [[Definition:Prime Number|prime]] with $p \divides \order G$.
Then $G$ has an element of [[Definition:Order of Group Element|order]] $p$.

substitutions.the prime p dividing the order: the prime power p^a dividing the order

derived.a subgroup of order p: a subgroup of order p^a, the case a = 1 recovering Cauchy
derived.the inductive step on the exponent: building up the p-power order one exponent at a time

object_map.reformulation: Promote the statement about a single prime factor to one about a full prime power, proved by induction on the exponent.

validity_conditions: Cauchy's theorem is the case a = 1, since a subgroup of order p is exactly the cyclic group generated by an element of order p.
The general case is proved by induction on the exponent, using Cauchy inside the normalizer quotient to enlarge a p-subgroup by one power at a time.
The normalizer step is essential: it is what supplies a normal subgroup to quotient by, and it has no counterpart in the a = 1 statement.
proof_plan: For $a = 1$, the result is [[Cauchy's Theorem (Group Theory)|Cauchy's Theorem]].

Let $H \le G$ with $\order H = p^i$, $i < a$.
Let $N = \map {N_G} H$ be its [[Definition:Normalizer|normalizer]].

By counting orbits of $H$ acting on the cosets $G / H$, $\index N H \equiv \index G H \pmod p$, so $p \divides \index N H$.
By [[Cauchy's Theorem (Group Theory)|Cauchy's Theorem]], $N / H$ has a subgroup of order $p$, whose preimage in $N$ is a subgroup of order $p^{i + 1}$ containing $H$.
